chunks: My father (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Sa'd ibn Abdillah narrated to me, who said: 'Abaad ibn Sulayman narrated to me from his father, from Harun ibn al-Jahm, from Ismail ibn Ammar al-Sayrafi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
I said: 'May I be your ransom, the believer is a mercy upon the believer.' He said: 'Yes.' I said: 'And how is that?'

He said: 'Whichever believer comes to his brother with a need, that is a mercy that Allah has directed to him and facilitated for him. If he fulfills the need, he has accepted the mercy by accepting it. And if he turns him away from his need while he is capable of fulfilling it, he has turned away from himself the mercy that Allah directed to him and facilitated for him, and the mercy is stored for him until the Day of Resurrection. Then the one who was turned away from his need will be the judge over it; if he wills, he directs it to himself, and if he wills, he directs it to another.'

'O Ismail, when it is the Day of Resurrection, he is the judge over the mercy of Allah, Exalted and Mighty, which has hastened for him. To whom do you think he will direct it?' I said: 'May I be your ransom, I would think he would direct it away from himself.'
He said: 'Do not think/guess, but be certain, for he will not direct it away from himself.'

'O Ismail, whoever comes to him with a need and he is capable of fulfilling it, but does not fulfill it for him, Allah will set loose a snake upon him which will bite his big toe in his grave until the Day of Resurrection, whether he is forgiven or punished.'

key_terms.إِبْهَامَهُ: His big toe (specifically the big toe of the foot)
key_terms.الْحَاکِمُ: The judge/decider (one who has authority over the stored mercy)
key_terms.رَحْمَهٌ: Mercy (divine favor/blessing directed to a person)
key_terms.شُجَاعاً: A snake (specifically a venomous one used as punishment)

ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual consequence for a believer who refuses to help another believer when capable?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Thawab al-A'mal*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) elucidates the spiritual mechanics of social support, framing the fulfillment of a believer's need as an active acceptance of divine mercy (*rahmah*) sent specifically through that interaction. The text highlights a profound eschatological consequence: refusing help while having the capacity to give results in the 'storage' of that missed mercy, which the individual will likely claim for themselves on the Day of Judgment, accompanied by a specific grave punishment (*adhab al-qabr*) symbolized by a snake biting the toe. This narrative underscores the Shia emphasis on *ta'awun* (mutual assistance) not merely as a social duty but as a critical mechanism for securing one's own spiritual reward and avoiding divine retribution.
